name: Paolo Veronese Green
lede: Paolo Veronese Green is a vivid blue-green named for the sixteenth-century Venetian painter Paolo Veronese, whose paintings are known for exactly this cool, saturated green in drapery and foliage.

sections.title: A painter's signature green
sections.body:
Paolo Veronese (1528-1588) was a major painter of the Venetian Renaissance, celebrated for large, color-saturated canvases in which a cool, vivid green recurs often enough in costume and landscape that later writers attached his name to the hue [1]. Our library's related entry for this family, *Sulphate Green Roll*, is dated by Maerz and Paul to 1905, which tells us the family of names was already settled by the early twentieth century, well after the painter's own lifetime [2]. The hex #009B7D measures a vivid bluish green by ISCC-NBS, 6.5 units from its nearest block, close to 9.0G 5.6/7.8 in Munsell notation [3]. The nearest named colors on file are [[illuminating-emerald]], [[ocean-green]] and [[zomp]], at 3.8, 
Whether Veronese mixed a single, specific pigment that this name preserves, or whether later writers simply named a recurring effect in his paintings after him, is not settled in the sources we checked, so we leave the distinction open rather than claim one side as fact [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to Paolo Veronese Green in only 5 of 23,781 paintings, 0.02 percent, with the within-painting test narrowing that to 2, making it rarer than about 82 percent of the named colors we track [4]. The earliest dated match, as photographed, comes from 1827, nearly two and a half centuries after the painter's death, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4]. The three earliest matches are credited to T. Davies rather than to Veronese himself [4]. That gap is a reminder that a color named for a painter need not actually appear, by our photographic measure, in that painter's own surviving work [4].

questions.q: Paolo Veronese Green is named for:
True or false: our archive's earliest match for this color is credited to Paolo Veronese himself.

openers: Its oldest match in our own archive isn't even attributed to the painter it's named for.
